# Trivy Offline Dependency Vulnerability Report (HIGH/CRITICAL to Strict CSV)

## Purpose
Generate a verifier-aligned vulnerability report for dependency or lock files using Trivy in offline mode, filtering to HIGH and CRITICAL findings only, exporting to a strict CSV schema, and validating the written artifact before completion.

## When to Use
Use when the task requires a machine-readable vulnerability report from dependency manifests/lockfiles (for example package-lock.json, yarn.lock, poetry.lock, requirements.txt) and the environment may be offline or air-gapped, with an explicit requirement to output a CSV with specific columns and to include only HIGH/CRITICAL findings.

## Procedure
- 1) Confirm requirements and inputs (no irreversible actions)
- Identify: (a) target file or directory to scan, (b) required output CSV path if specified, (c) whether network access is allowed (unknown is treated as offline).
- Validate the target exists and is readable. If ambiguous (multiple candidate lockfiles), stop and ask for the intended target rather than guessing.
- 2) Discover tools and offline DB cache (environment grounding)
- Check Trivy availability (for example, locate the executable via PATH). If missing, stop with an install instruction appropriate to the environment (do not assume apt/wget).
- Discover a usable Trivy cache directory by checking candidate locations in this order:
- user-provided cache dir (if any)
- $TRIVY_CACHE_DIR (if set)
- $XDG_CACHE_HOME/trivy (if set)
- $HOME/.cache/trivy (if set)
- a writable working-directory cache (only if writable)
- A cache is usable only if it contains db/trivy.db (and preferably db/metadata.json).
- Decision point:
- If a usable cache is found, proceed offline.
- If no usable cache is found:
- If network is explicitly allowed, perform a DB fetch step once (download-db-only) into a chosen writable cache dir, then re-check that db/trivy.db exists.
- If network is not allowed or unknown, stop and report that an offline DB seed is required, including the exact cache dir structure expected (db/trivy.db).
- 3) Run Trivy scan with strict offline and severity constraints
- Run Trivy against the discovered target using offline flags and HIGH/CRITICAL filtering:
- Must include: --offline-scan and --skip-db-update and --cache-dir <chosen_cache_dir>
- Must include: --severity HIGH,CRITICAL
- Choose output format as JSON for parsing (not as the final deliverable).
- Checkpoint: verify the command exit code indicates success; if not, capture stderr/stdout and stop (do not fabricate a report).
- 4) Transform scan results into the required CSV schema
- Parse the JSON and emit a CSV with exactly these columns (header required):
- Package,Version,CVE_ID,Severity,CVSS_Score,Fixed_Version,Title,Url
- Mapping rules (do not guess values):
- Package: package name field from the finding
- Version: installed version
- CVE_ID: vulnerability identifier
- Severity: must be HIGH or CRITICAL
- CVSS_Score: pick one numeric score if present; otherwise emit N/A
- Fixed_Version: fixed version if present; else N/A
- Title: title if present; else N/A
- Url: primary URL if present; else N/A
- Dedup rule: if the same (Package, Version, CVE_ID) appears multiple times, keep one row (prefer the row with a non-N/A CVSS_Score or Url).
- 5) Write the CSV to the required location (output grounding)
- If the task/verifier specifies an output path, write exactly there. Do not silently change the path.
- If no path is specified, write to a clearly named file in the working directory and report its path.
- Checkpoint: confirm the file exists and is readable after writing.
- 6) Validate the produced CSV (schema validation anchor)
- Reload the written CSV and assert:
- Header includes all required columns in the schema (order may be preserved if required by the task; otherwise do not reorder arbitrarily).
- Every row has Severity in {HIGH, CRITICAL}. If any other value appears, fail and fix the filter/transform rather than shipping.
- CSV is parseable as comma-separated values and contains a header row even when there are zero findings.
- Report counts: total_rows, high_count, critical_count.

## Constraints / Pitfalls
- Never assume a specific cache path (for example ./trivy-cache or /root/trivy-cache). Discover or accept a user-provided cache directory, and verify db/trivy.db exists before running offline.
- Do not rely on network downloads unless network access is explicitly allowed; in offline/unknown conditions, fail fast with an actionable message rather than attempting download-db-only.

# vulnerability-csv-reporting

## Purpose
Generate a verifier-visible CSV security audit report from vulnerability scan data by discovering inputs in the live environment, applying an explicit filter and field mapping, writing the CSV to the task-required path, and validating the produced artifact by reloading it and asserting schema/shape before claiming completion.

## When to Use
Use this skill when a task requires producing a CSV report from vulnerability findings (often JSON from a scanner) and the environment expects an actual file on disk at a specific path. Do not use for narrative security summaries or when the required output is not a CSV artifact.

## Procedure
- Step 1: Discover requirements and paths before doing work
- Identify the required output CSV path from the task/verifier; if none is specified, ask or discover a conventional location and confirm it.
- Discover the available inputs by listing the working directory and locating candidate vulnerability data files (for example, *.json, scanner output directories).
- Checkpoint: confirm the input file you will parse exists and is readable (size > 0), and confirm you have write permission to the output directory.
- Step 2: Ground tool availability and choose the minimal working route
- Prefer Python for parsing and CSV writing (standard library). Verify availability: run python3 --version or python --version via the terminal tool.
- If python3 is missing but python exists, use python. If neither exists, stop and request an environment-supported alternative rather than emitting unexecuted code.
- Optional: if you intend to run a scanner first, verify the scanner binary exists and that required flags are supported; otherwise, proceed with converting existing scan output only.
- Step 3: Convert findings to CSV records (mapping + filtering)
- Inspect the top-level structure of the input JSON (print keys and a small sample) to avoid hard-coded assumptions.
- Define the CSV header (fieldnames) explicitly and keep it stable.
- Implement a mapping function that:
- Produces exactly one flat dict per vulnerability row.
- Uses safe defaults (for example, N/A) when fields are missing or null.
- Applies the requested severity filter only if the task asks for it; otherwise include all severities.
- Decision point: if the expected vulnerabilities list is missing (for example, no "Vulnerabilities" key or it is empty), still write a CSV with the header row and zero data rows unless the task requires otherwise.
- Step 4: Write the CSV to the required path using an actual terminal tool call
- Write via Python csv.DictWriter with newline="" and UTF-8 encoding.
- Do not paste a "tool call" blob into chat. Execute the write using the platform terminal tool so the file is created on disk.
- Checkpoint: the command must exit successfully (return code 0) before proceeding.
- Step 5: Post-write verification (must pass before finalizing) [EXECUTION ANCHOR]
- In the terminal tool, verify the artifact is present at the exact required path:
- ls -l <csv_path> (or equivalent) shows the file exists and is non-empty if rows were expected.
- Reload and validate the CSV schema/shape using Python:
- Assert the first row header equals the expected fieldnames exactly (same names and order).
- Assert every subsequent row has exactly the same number of columns as the header.
- If severity filtering is requested, assert all output Severity values are within the requested set.
- If any assertion fails: do not claim success; fix mapping/header/paths and re-run only the minimal failing step, then re-run this verification.

## Constraints / Pitfalls
- Never claim the report is generated unless the CSV exists and is readable at the task-specified output path and the post-write reload validation passes. Do not silently write to a different directory if permission/path issues occur; instead, diagnose and resolve or ask.
- Avoid brittle assumptions about scanner JSON structure (fixed keys, nested shapes, or CVSS locations). Always inspect the input structure first and implement a single bounded fallback for missing keys (write header-only CSV or map alternate key paths) rather than expanding into an unbounded troubleshooting guide.

# Dependency Security Audit CSV (Trivy JSON to CSV)

## Purpose
Produce a verifier-aligned security audit CSV by scanning a project for vulnerabilities, extracting CVE and CVSS data with stable fallbacks, filtering to the required severities, writing the CSV to the task-specified path, and validating the artifact and schema before finishing.

## When to Use
Use this when a task requires a machine-readable CSV deliverable (often at a specific path) summarizing HIGH/CRITICAL vulnerabilities from a dependency scan (commonly Trivy), including identifiers, package info, CVSS score selection, and remediation fields.

## Procedure
- Step 1: Discover the contract and inputs (do not assume)
- Identify the required output path and required CSV columns from the task statement; if either is not explicit, pause and infer from nearby task scaffolding (e.g., README, provided verifier script) or ask for clarification.
- Discover the dependency target(s): locate lockfiles/manifests by listing the working directory and searching for common files (package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, requirements.txt, poetry.lock, Pipfile.lock, go.mod, Cargo.lock, Gemfile.lock).
- Check tool availability: confirm whether a scanner (prefer Trivy) exists in PATH; if not, look for an allowed alternative already present (do not install unless explicitly allowed).
- Step 2: Run a scan with a reproducible, inspectable output
- Run the scanner in a mode that emits structured output (JSON preferred) and captures dependency vulnerabilities for the discovered target.
- Save the raw scan output to a local file (path discovered at runtime); record how to reproduce it.
- Checkpoint: confirm the JSON file exists and is parseable (load it with a JSON parser). If parse fails, re-run with correct output flags or switch scanner mode.
- Step 3: Parse and normalize vulnerability records (schema-driven)
- Load the JSON and discover where vulnerabilities live (commonly Results[*].Vulnerabilities[*]); do not hard-code the nesting until confirmed by inspection of keys.
- For each vulnerability record, construct a normalized row object using the required CSV columns; typical fields include:
- Vulnerability ID (e.g., CVE), package name, installed version, fixed version (or "N/A"), severity, title/description, URL, CVSS score, CVSS version, CVSS source.
- CVSS selection rule (keep minimal, behavior-changing logic):
- Prefer CVSS v3/v3.1 base score when present; use source priority: nvd then ghsa then redhat (only among sources actually present in the record).
- If no v3 score exists, optionally fall back to v2 score from the highest-priority available source (commonly nvd) if the task allows; otherwise set "N/A".
- Accept only numeric scores (int/float); otherwise treat as missing and continue fallback.
- URL selection fallback:
- Prefer a primary URL field if present (often PrimaryURL).
- Else use the first item in a References list/array if present.
- Else set "N/A".
- Filtering decision point:
- Apply the task-required filter. If the requirement is "HIGH and CRITICAL only", filter by severity label (case-insensitive match).
- If the requirement is score-threshold-based, filter by numeric CVSS when available; if missing, fall back to severity label only if the task explicitly permits.
- Checkpoint: report counts (total vulns found, rows after filtering). If zero rows remain, keep going (still write a CSV with header), but note the reason.
- Step 4: Write CSV to the required path and validate (hard completion gate)
- Write the CSV to the exact task-specified output path. Do not silently change directories or substitute a different path.
- Use a CSV writer that quotes/escapes fields and writes a single header row matching the required column names exactly.
- Post-write validation (must pass before completion):
- Existence/readability: stat and read the file from the exact required path.
- Schema: parse the CSV back in and assert the header contains all required columns (and no unexpected header mismatches if the contract is exact).
- Content: assert every row satisfies the filter condition (e.g., severity in {HIGH, CRITICAL}); assert CVSS values are either numeric or "N/A" per schema.
- Sanity: if the scan reported at least one HIGH/CRITICAL vuln, assert row count > 0; otherwise allow 0 rows but keep header.
- If any validation fails: do not claim completion. Fix mapping, filter logic, or write location, then re-run Step 4.

## Constraints / Pitfalls
- Never assume JSON schema, vulnerability nesting, required CSV headers, or output path; always discover from task instructions and by inspecting the scan output before coding the parser.
- Do not complete until the CSV is written to the exact required path and passes a reload-and-assert validation (existence, header/schema, and filter correctness); printing to stdout or writing to an alternate path is not acceptable.
